#  Question 1

## Data Loading and cleaning

```{r}
# Loading household_expenditure.csv and saving it as a tibble with its name as house

house <- read_csv("data/household_expenditure.csv")
```


The data dictionary of the loaded household_expenditure.csv file



Variable        | Description                                                                 
----------------|---------------------------------
Kids            | Number of kids in the household
HouseholdSize   | Number of people in Household
Sex             | Gender of the survey respondent
Vehicles        | Number of vehicles in the household
Food            | Average food expenditure per week
Housing         | Average amount spent on accommodation per week
Alcohol         | Average alcohol expenditure per week
Debt            | Average amount spent on debt payment per week
income_category | Income category of the household

```{r}
# Checking the summary of the house tibble

summary(house)
```
The given dataset has about 4097 records. Upon checking the summary of the house tibble. It is seen that Kids, HouseholdSize and Debt columns have 6, 6 and 8 NA values recorded respectively. Some records are missing more than one of these, so removing them drops 14 records, which reduces the records to 4083.

```{r}
house_clean <- house %>%
  filter(!is.na(Kids), !is.na(HouseholdSize), !is.na(Debt))

summary(house_clean)
```
```{r}
# Checking the uniqueness of the data to see if there are case errors or misspellings

unique(house_clean$Sex)
unique(house_clean$income_category)
```

There are no issues in Sex and income_category variables.

```{r}
# Converting Sex and income_category to categorical data

house_clean <- house_clean %>%
  mutate(Sex=factor(Sex),
         income_category=factor(income_category, c('Low', 'Medium', 'High')))
         
```

## Variable visualisations

The distribution of each variables is checked, along with its mean to check out if there are any huge outliers. 

```{r}
mean_data <- house_clean %>%
  group_by(income_category) %>%
  summarise(food_mean = mean(Food),
            housing_mean = mean(Housing),
            alcohol_mean = mean(Alcohol),
            debt_mean = mean(Debt))
```


```{r}

ggplot(house_clean, aes(factor(Kids))) +

```

In figure 1, it can be seen that regardless of income category, most households have 0 kids.

```{r}
# Plotting frequency distribution of household size

ggplot(house_clean, aes(factor(HouseholdSize))) +

```

In figure 2,most households with low income have 1-2 people living, in medium income household it is 1-3 people living and in large income household 2-3 people are living.

```{r}
# Plotting frequency distribution of number of vehicles

ggplot(house_clean, aes(factor(Vehicles))) +

  facet_wrap(income_category~.) +

```

In figure 3, it can be seen that regardless of income category, most households have 0-2 vehicles.

Some households in low and medium income have outlier households with spending over 600 pounds on housing.These records are not removed as it is not too far from mean and does not change the distribution.

## Statistical testing

The correlation is calculated for each variable to see if there are any highly correlated data. If there are, it would lead to multicollinearity.

```{r}
# Calculating the correlation between variables

rcorr(as.matrix(select_if(house_clean, is.numeric)))
```


Most data do not have high correlation with each other except for Kids and HouseholdSize. This is expected since household size will include kids also.

### Effect of variables upon food expenditure

To examine the effects of the number of kids, household size, income category, alcohol expenditure, debt payment, housing payment and number of vehicles on food expenditure, a multiple linear regression model is fitted with these variables. Sex variable is not considered in this and further analysis because it is the gender of the survey respondent. The gender of the respondent does not normally change expenditure of household, the size and number of vehicles. Kids is also removed, since it is highly corelated with household size. 

```{r}
m.food <- lm(Food~ HouseholdSize+income_category+ Alcohol+ Debt+ Housing+Vehicles, data = house_clean)
summary(m.food)
```

```{r}
cbind(coef(m.food),confint(m.food))
```

Upon running the model, it is seen that  Alcohol, Housing and debt have very high significance effect on food expenditure. 

The housing expenditure is the most significant, showing that with a pound extra spent on housing, the food expenditure will increase by 0.09 pounds ($b = 0.09$, CI = [0.08, 0.09], $t(4075)=26.25$, $p<0.001$). While with 1 pound extra spent on alcohol will food expenditure by 0.38 pounds ($b = 0.38$, CI = [0.26, 0.51], $t(4075)=6.23$, $p<0.001$) and with 1 pound extra spent on debt payment, will decrease the food expenditure by 0.05 pounds ($b = -0.05$, CI = [-0.06, -0.03], $t(4075)=-5.05$, $p<0.001$).

The household size and number of vehicles are not a significant predictor for food expenditure. But in income category, the households with medium category income is shown to be marginally significant with 1.04 pounds increase in food expenditure compared to low income category households ($b = 1.05$, CI = [0.15, 1.95], $t(4075)=2.28$, $p=0.023$) but households with high income category is not shown to be significantly different from low income households.

### Effects of alcohol and whether the effect is the same across households with different debt payments

The interaction effect of Alcohol and Debt with effects of other variables on food expenditure is examined using linear regression model

```{r}
m.food.int <- lm(Food~ HouseholdSize+income_category+Alcohol*Debt+ Housing+Vehicles , data = house_clean)
summary(m.food.int)
``` 

```{r}
vif(m.food.int)
```

The VIF scores of Debt and Alcohol variables are very high, despite having very less correlation. This is a structural multicollinearity. To combat this alcohol and debt is normalised.

```{r}
house_clean <- house_clean %>%
  mutate(nAlcohol=Alcohol-mean(Alcohol),
         nDebt=Debt-mean(Debt))

m.food.int <- lm(Food~ HouseholdSize+income_category+nAlcohol*nDebt+ Housing+Vehicles , data = house_clean)
summary(m.food.int)


```

```{r}
vif(m.food.int)
```
The VIF scores low, so the model is good.

```{r}
cbind(coef(m.food.int),confint(m.food.int))
```

Upon seeing the interactions between alcohol expenditure and debt payments and effects of other variables on food expenditure, it is shown that the interaction is not significant ($b = -0.0015$, CI = [-0.008, 0.005], $t(4074)=-0.49$, $p=0.62$) . This indicates that the effect of alcohol expenditure on food expenditure does not significantly differ across different debt payment levels.



Now, the interaction effect of alcohol expenditure and debt payment on food expenditure without the effects of other variables, to see if significance changes without other variables.

```{r}
m.food.int2 <- lm(Food~ nAlcohol*nDebt , data = house_clean)
summary(m.food.int2)
```
```{r}
cbind(coef(m.food.int2),confint(m.food.int2))
```

The significance of the interaction in this model has increased ($b = -0.003$, CI = [-0.010, 0.003], $t(4079)=-0.92$, $p=0.36$) compared to previous model, but it still doesn't reject the null hypothesis. On the surface this model might be better but the F-statistic score is much lower. 

The anova model is now used to see which model is better.

```{r}
anova(m.food.int, m.food.int2)
```

The result of the anova model is very significant and it shows Model 1, which includes other variables, fits much better compared to Model 2 with just interaction effect between alcohol and debt variables ($F(5,4074)=140.24$, $p<0.001$). This shows that we cannot ignore other variables like housing expenditure, to gain understanding of food expenditure even if we are just seeing interaction effect of the said variables.

# Question 2

## Data Loading and cleaning

```{r}
# Loading the podcast_listens.csv and saving it as a tibble with its name as podcast

podcast <- read_csv("data/podcast_listens.csv")
```


The data dictionary of the loaded podcast_listens.csv file.



Variable            | Description                                                                 
--------------------|---------------------------------
Platform            | The platform where the podcast is being streamed
genre               | Genre of podcast
avg.review          | Average review rating of the podcast
daily.listens       |  Average daily listens
total.reviews       | Number of reviews the podcast has
subscribers         | Subscriber count of the podcast

```{r}
# Checking the summary of the podcast tibble

summary(podcast)
```
The podcast dataset has about 5400 records of data. From the summary, it is seen that the subscribers data has records which have less than 0 subscribers and is in decimals. This is not possible since this is not average and total count cannot be less than zero. It is also seen that avg.review has readings with 100, while majority of data are less than 5 as we can see from quartiles. This means the rating score is out of 5. 

So the subscribers less than 0 and avg.reviews over 5 are removed. Also the subscribers are rounded and Platform and genre are made into categorical.


```{r}
podcast_clean <- podcast %>%
  mutate(subscribers=round(subscribers),
         Platform=factor(Platform),
         genre=factor(genre, c("Documentary","Comedy","News & Culture"))) %>%
  filter(subscribers>=0) %>% 
  filter(avg.review<=5) 

summary(podcast_clean)
```


## Variable visualisations

The distribution of each variables are checked, along with its mean to check out any huge outliers. 

```{r}
# Checking the uniqueness of the data to see there are case errors or misspellings

unique(podcast_clean$Platform)

unique(podcast_clean$genre)
```

There are no issues in platform and genre columns


```{r}
#calculating the mean for the plots

mean_pod_data <- podcast_clean  %>%
  summarise(avgreview_mean = mean(avg.review),
            listens_mean = mean(daily.listens),
            totreview_mean = mean(total.reviews),
            subs_mean = mean(subscribers))
```

```{r}
# Plotting frequency distribution of average review

ggplot(podcast_clean, aes(avg.review))+
  geom_histogram( bins=30, color='black', alpha=0.4) +  
  geom_vline(data = mean_pod_data, aes(xintercept = avgreview_mean, linetype = "Mean"), color='red') + 
  scale_linetype_manual(
    name = 'Statistics', 
    values = c("Mean" = "dashed")
  )+
  labs(y="Frequency", x="Average review rating", title = "Fig 8:- Frequency distribution of Average review rating ")
```


In figure 8, it can be seen that on average, the review ratings of podcast is around 4.3. There are also couple of podcast with zero score. On the surface, this is not an issue, but will be investigated further latter.




```{r}
# Plotting frequency distribution of daily listens

ggplot(podcast_clean, aes(daily.listens))+
  geom_histogram(color='black', alpha=0.4, bins=40) + 
  geom_vline(data = mean_pod_data, aes(xintercept = listens_mean, linetype = "Mean"), color='red') + 
  scale_linetype_manual(
    name = 'Statistics', 
    values = c("Mean" = "dashed")
  ) +
  labs(y="Frequency", x="Average daily listens", title = "Fig 9:-Frequency distribution of average daily listens")
```

In figure 9, it can be seen that on average, the daily listens of podcast is around 4500.


```{r}
# Plotting frequency distribution of total reviews

ggplot(podcast_clean, aes(total.reviews))+
  geom_histogram(color='black', alpha=0.4) +
  geom_vline(data = mean_pod_data, aes(xintercept = totreview_mean, linetype = "Mean"), color='red') + 
  scale_linetype_manual(
    name = 'Statistics', 
    values = c("Mean" = "dashed")
  ) +
  labs(y="Frequency", x="Total Reviews", title = "Fig 10:-Frequency distribution of total review")
```

In figure 10, on average a podcast has about 900 reviews. It is also seen that there is a significant outlier for podcast with no reviews. This will be investigated further later on along with avg.reviews.



```{r}
# Plotting frequency distribution of total subscribers

ggplot(podcast_clean, aes(subscribers))+
  geom_histogram(color='black', alpha=0.4) +
  geom_vline(data = mean_pod_data, aes(xintercept = subs_mean, linetype = "Mean"), color='red') + 
  scale_linetype_manual(
    name = 'Statistics', 
    values = c("Mean" = "dashed")
  ) + 
  labs(y="Frequency", x="Total Subscribers", title = "Fig 11:- Frequency distribution of Total Subscribers ")
```

In figure 11, on average, a podcast has around 600 subscribers.

```{r}
# Plotting average review vs total reviews

ggplot(podcast_clean, aes(total.reviews, avg.review)) +  geom_point() + 
  labs(y="Average Review Score", x="Total Reviews", title = "Fig 12:- Average Review Score vs Number of Reviews")
```

In Figure 12, it is seen that podcast with 0 reviews and score is huge outlier. These podcast will be removed only in upcoming analysis on effect of average review score and total reviews on daily listens and not on other analysis, because it still contains other important information.

## Statistical testing

The correlation is calculated for each variable to see if there are any highly correlated data. If there are, it would lead to multicollinearity.

```{r}
rcorr(as.matrix(select_if(podcast_clean, is.numeric)))
```
There is very little correlation each variable. And the correlations of avg.review and subscribers and daily.listens and avg.review correlation very close to zero. Which means they have almost no relation with each other.

### Do podcasts have more/fewer listens depending upon their average review scores and total number of reviews.

To examine the effects of average review and total reviews on daily listens, a multiple linear regression model is fitted with these variables. As stated above, the records with 0 total reviews and average reviews are filtered out, as it is a huge outlier.


```{r}
podcast.new <- podcast_clean%>% 
  filter(total.reviews>0) %>%
  filter(avg.review>0)


m.listen <- lm(daily.listens~avg.review + total.reviews, data=podcast.new)

summary(m.listen)
```



```{r}
cbind(coef(m.listen),confint(m.listen))
```
On running the multiple regression model on average review score and total reviews, it is seen that total reviews of the podcast is shown to have significant effect on average daily listens, with a unit increase in total reviews will increase the listens by 0.21 per day ($b = 0.21$, CI = [0.18, 0.24], $t(5350)=13.16$, $p<0.001$).

Whereas, average review score is not have a significant effect on daily listens, which indicates that review scores doesn't significantly change daily listens. This relation can also be seen in correlation matrix, which is very close to zero.

### Contrast the effect of listens across different genres.


To see daily listens on each genre, a linear regression model with them.
```{r}
m.listen.genre <- lm(daily.listens~genre, data=podcast_clean)
summary(m.listen.genre)
```

```{r}
cbind(coef(m.listen.genre),confint(m.listen.genre))
```


Here the documentary genre is used as reference category for the model.

From the regression output, it can be seen that Comedy has on average 351 more views than Documentary ($b = 351$, CI = [342.60, 359.16], $t(5373)=83.04$, $p<0.001$), while News and Culture genre has on average has 150 more views than Documentary ($b = 149.76$, CI = [141.48, 158.05], $t(5373)=35.44$, $p<0.001$).

```{r}
(m.listen.genre.emm <- emmeans(m.listen.genre, ~genre))
```

```{r}
(  m.listen.genre.pairs <- confint(pairs(m.listen.genre.emm))  )
```



```{r, fig.width=12}
emm_pod <- ggplot(summary(m.listen.genre.emm), aes(x=genre,y=emmean,ymin=lower.CL, ymax=upper.CL)) + geom_linerange(linewidth=1) + geom_point(color="red") + labs(x="Genre", y="Daily Listens", title="Average daily listens across Genre ",subtitle="Error bars are 95% CIs")

cont_pod <- ggplot(m.listen.genre.pairs, aes(x=contrast, y=estimate, ymin=lower.CL, ymax=upper.CL)) + geom_linerange(linewidth=1) + geom_point(color="red") + labs(x="Contrasts", y="Difference in Daily Listens", title="Contrasts of daily listens across Genre ",subtitle="Error bars are 95% CIs")

grid.arrange(emm_pod, cont_pod, ncol=2, top = textGrob("Fig13:-Average and contrasts of daily listens across genre"))
```

The left plot of Figure 13 shows the mean daily listens for each genre. Comedy has the most daily listens, followed by News&Culture. The documentary genre has the lowest listens. The right plot shows the estimated differences in daily listens for each sets of genre. 

### What is the effect of subscribers upon the number of listens, and is this different across genres?

To examine the effects of subscribers on the number of listens for each genre, a multiple linear regression model is fitted with the interaction of subscribers and genre.


```{r}
m.subscribers <- lm(daily.listens~subscribers*genre, data=podcast_clean)
summary(m.subscribers)

```

```{r}
vif(m.subscribers)
```
The VIF scores of subscribers is very high when interacting with genre, despite having very less correlation. This is a structural multicollinearity. To combat this subscribers is normalised.


```{r}
podcast_clean <- podcast_clean %>%
  mutate(nsubscribers=subscribers-mean(subscribers))

m.subscribers <- lm(daily.listens~nsubscribers*genre, data=podcast_clean)
summary(m.subscribers)
```

```{r}
vif(m.subscribers)
```
The VIF score is less than 10, which is good now.


```{r}
cbind(coef(m.subscribers),confint(m.subscribers))
```

The total subscribers have a significant positive effect on daily listens, with every new subscriber there will be 0.24 increase daily listens when seeing baseline documentary category ($b = 0.24$, CI = [0.2, 0.29], $t(5370)=11.28$, $p<0.001$).

The model also shows that there is significant change in listens when comparing with other genres. For comedy genre, for every new subscriber there will be 0.32 increase in daily listens (0.08 increase from documentary genre) ($b = 0.08$, CI = [0.02, 0.14], $t(5370)=2.53$, $p=0.012$). Whereas for News&Culture genre, for every new subscriber, there will be 0.38 increase in daily listens ($b = 0.13$, CI = [0.07, 0.19], $t(5370)=4.362$, $p<0.001$).

The effects of subscribers on daily listens for each genre can be seen in below figure.

```{r}
ggplot(podcast_clean, aes(x=subscribers, y=daily.listens, colour = genre)) +  geom_smooth(method = lm, se=FALSE) + 
  labs(y="Daily Listens", x="Total Subscribers", title = "Fig 14:- Daily Listens vs Subscribers for each genre")
```

In figure 14, it can be seen that there is positive relation between susbcribers and daily listens for all 3 genres.The comedy genre is the most popular, with having more daily listens for the same amount if subscribers compared to other genre. At 500 subscribers, the comedy genre gets around 4700 daily listens, News & Culture gets around 4500 daily listens, and Documentary gets around 4300 daily listens. Since each extra subscriber adds more listens for News & Culture than for Comedy, News & Culture could eventually catch up with Comedy at very high subscriber counts, although this would be extrapolating beyond the data.
